entry.hook: Ying Gou (噬天赢勾 — Heaven-Devouring Ying Gou) was not transformed by an enemy’s blade, but by his own refusal to forgive himself. A half-human, half-Wu general under the war-god Chiyou, he made one fatal error on the battlefield, and his entire elite clan was annihilated within three days—every soldier dead, and he alone escaped. Unable to bear the weight of that survival, he tore out his own soul and implanted it into a corpse body refined by the sealed zombie progenitor Jiang Chen, believing that by becoming a dead thing he could somehow repay the debt. What he discovered instead was a prison without an exit: an undying vessel that would not let him die, a curse that would not let him be forgiven, and a hatred aimed at the only target he could never destroy—himself.

body.body_1:
Heaven-Devouring Ying Gou / 噬天赢勾 (Ying Gou, the Self-Devourer)  
Corruption Source: 复仇的执念 (The All-Consuming Need for Revenge Against the One Who Betrayed Him — where the betrayer is himself)  
Conversion Era: Late Honghuang Era, during the war between Chiyou and the Yellow Emperor Xuan Yuan  
Current Mo Grade: Obsession-Bound (执念缠身者)  
Sphere of Influence: Ancient battlefields, desolate wastelands, and the memory-saturated ruins of the Yellow Emperor–Chiyou war
body.body_2: Ying Gou belongs to the initial grade of Mo hierarchy: the Obsession-Bound. In this stage, the original self has not yet been fully consumed or replaced by the fixation—the person is still recognizably himself, but the obsession has become the central axis around which all thought and action revolve. He has existed in this state for approximately five thousand years since his voluntary transformation into a zombie body. The core feature of this grade is the preservation of the original identity alongside a single, unshakeable conviction that the self is guilty and must be punished. Ying Gou’s obsession is unique: it is not directed outward toward any other being, but inward, forming a closed loop of self-condemnation that can never be resolved because the accused and the judge are the same entity.
body.body_3:
Ying Gou’s descent was neither accidental nor forced. Before his fall, he was a renowned general serving under Chiyou (蚩尤), the primordial war god. As a hybrid of human and Wu bloodlines, he commanded a mixed elite force known for its ferocity and loyalty. During a key campaign against the Yellow Emperor’s army, Ying Gou misjudged the terrain and the timing of an ambush. His entire elite clan—three thousand warriors—was encircled and annihilated over three days. He alone escaped through a gap in the enemy formation, wounded but alive.  

The moment of conversion occurred not on the battlefield but later, in solitude, when the full weight of his survival hit him. He sat among the bones of his fallen soldiers, repeating their names. The realization that he—their commander—had walked out while they were slaughtered became an unbearable contradiction. He tried to take his own life, but his hybrid constitution made natural death nearly impossible. Desperate, he traveled to the sealed cavern where the legendary corpse-refiner Jiang Chen (将臣) lay imprisoned. He offered himself: “Turn me into one of them. I have no right to breathe.” Jiang Chen, sensing the opportunity to spread his cursed art, obliged. Ying Gou’s soul was forcibly extracted and implanted into a corpse body refined by Jiang Chen. The transformation was immediate and irreversible. His lungs no longer drew air. His heart stopped. But his consciousness remained, trapped in a vessel that would not decay and would not die.
body.body_4:
Ying Gou’s obsession manifests as a single, recursive thought: “I should have died with them. I am not allowed to live.” This thought plays in an endless loop, day and night, for five thousand years. It is not a momentary regret but a gnawing, ever-present conviction that colors every perception.  

The zombie body he now inhabits distorts his sensory world in a specific manner: he no longer perceives the warmth of living things, only the cold stillness of death. The breath of a living person feels to him like a reproach; the pulse of blood reminds him of what he failed to protect. He has developed an acute sensitivity to the echoes of violence—locations where large numbers died retain a kind of “imprint” that he can feel as a low hum. These sites draw him, not because he enjoys suffering, but because the collective weight of death feels more honest than the fragile vitality of the living.  

The obsession is irreversible because it is logically self-sealing: he cannot forgive himself because he believes he does not deserve forgiveness; and because he cannot die, he has no way to exit the loop. Any attempt to argue with the obsession only strengthens it—every moment he remains alive is fresh evidence of his guilt.
body.body_5:
Unlike many Mo who develop the insatiable hunger known as Wu Yun Chi Sheng (五蕴炽盛), Ying Gou does not crave fear, blood, or emotional essence. His zombie body does not require sustenance in the ordinary sense, and his obsession does not express itself through physical appetite. Instead, he suffers from a different kind of deprivation: the hunger for atonement.  

He collects the broken weapons and bones of the dead from ancient battlefields, carrying them to secluded valleys where he builds mounds—empty graves. Each mound is a ritual: he arranges the fragments into the shape of a fallen warrior, then leaves without looking back. The act brings a temporary numbness, a few hours or days of quiet. But soon the thought returns: “These are not my soldiers. These are strangers. My soldiers died because of me, and I did not even build them proper graves.” The numbness curdles into a deeper emptiness, and the cycle begins again—wandering, collecting, building, failing.  

In rare moments of clarity, Ying Gou examines his own reflection in still water. He sees a corpse face, frozen in the expression of the moment he died—a grimace of self-loathing. He knows exactly what he has become. He knows that the transformation was his own choice. That clarity is the most unbearable part: there is no excuse, no monster he can blame. He did this to himself.
body.body_6:
Ying Gou has not reached the stage of Yan Mo (魇魔). His obsession has not coalesced into an independent consciousness that speaks to him or attempts to seize control. He remains a single identity—the same person who made the mistake, who sought the transformation, who now wanders the desolate lands.  

However, a subtle internal division exists. There is “the should-have-died commander” and “the zombie who is still walking.” These two perspectives coexist within one mind. The commander judges the zombie for every step it takes; the zombie silently bears the judgment because it knows it deserves it. There is no struggle for dominance because both agree on the verdict: guilty. There is no rebellion from an obsession-entity because the obsession and the self are perfectly aligned. This is the unique tragedy of Ying Gou: his Mo is not a parasite but a mirror.
body.body_7:
Ying Gou’s existence is defined not by large-scale destruction but by a kind of mournful persistence. His most notable acts are the construction of empty burial mounds across the northern plains—sites that later became known as “Ying Gou’s Monuments” among local folk traditions. Hundreds of these mounds dot the wasteland, each containing the rusted armor, shattered spears, and sun-bleached skulls of anonymous dead.  

There is no record of direct conflict with Heaven or any celestial army. Because Ying Gou does not attack the living or disrupt the natural order beyond his self-imposed wandering, the Celestial Court has largely ignored him. One Daoist hermit’s journal from the Han dynasty describes an encounter: “A figure in black, walking alone through the field of bones. It did not speak. It did not threaten. It picked up a broken sword, held it for a long moment, then placed it on a growing pile. I could not look away. There was such weight in that gesture.”  

His only documented violence occurred when a bandit group tried to loot one of his mounds. According to the account, he turned to face them, and the mere sight of his face—not his actions—caused the bandits to flee screaming. The survivors later described his expression as “the face of a man who has already died so many times inside that his body forgot to follow.”
body.body_8:
**Relationship with the Daoist path:** Ying Gou was never a Daoist cultivator; his martial training came from the Wu war traditions and the hybrid bloodline. Post-transformation, Daoist exorcists have occasionally attempted to perform rites to lay his soul to rest, but these have always failed—his soul is already bound to a zombie body and refuses any form of release that could be mistaken for forgiveness.  

**Relationship with the Divine path:** The Celestial Court has not formally classified him as a target of suppression. He does not threaten cosmic order, nor does he spread chaos. Several regional earth gods (土地神) have been recorded as feeling “uneasy” in his presence but report no aggressive behavior.  

**Relationship with the Buddhist path:** No records exist of Buddhist intervention. His obsession is inward-facing, and the Buddhist doctrine of releasing attachment is the very thing he cannot accept—releasing his guilt would mean releasing his only form of penitence.  

**Relationship with the demonic and mortal realms:** Among the growing ranks of Jiang Shi (僵尸) and lesser undead, Ying Gou is occasionally recognized as a kind of elder, but he does not lead or command. Mortal folklore remembers him as a sorrowful figure: some villages leave offerings of broken weapons at crossroads, hoping he will take them and build another mound, thereby sparing their own dead from being disturbed.
body.body_9:
Ying Gou remains active. He has not been sealed, imprisoned, or destroyed. He continues to wander the battlefields of the ancient north, collecting fragments of the dead and building his empty graves. He has not triggered Tian Qian (天谴), the celestial obliteration reserved for Mo that directly threaten cosmic law. His existence, though tragic, operates within a narrow scope: he harms no one but himself, and his obsession is ultimately a form of self-grounding rather than outward chaos.  

The Daoist cosmic order does not have a formal category for a being like him—a Mo who does not feed on life, does not corrupt reality, does not rebel. Some scholars of demonology have argued that Ying Gou is not truly Mo but a “failed ghost” or “unfinished corpse.” The tradition, however, has always counted him among the four great zombie progenitors. In the moral accounting of the universe, Ying Gou’s current state is an open wound that has not been closed and may never be closed. He is not a lesson and not a warning—he is simply a man who could not let himself live, and the cosmos, indifferent to his suffering, let him have his wish.
body.body_10: The most recognized remnants are the “Ying Gou Mounds” (赢勾冢), a loosely connected chain of hundreds of small burial mounds scattered across the northern plains of China, particularly in the region south of the Yin Mountains. Local legends vary: some say the mounds mark the graves of his fallen soldiers; others claim they are graves for random strangers he found along his path. The one constant is that none contain the bones of a single identifiable victim—they are all anonymous, assembled from the debris of forgotten wars. No central site is known to hold any part of Ying Gou himself.
body.body_11: The description of Ying Gou’s relationship with the Daoist and divine orders is informed by the broader framework of the Celestial Court’s treatment of passive Mo. For the relationship between Ying Gou and his creator Jiang Chen, see the entry on Jiang Chen (将臣). For the war god under whom he once served, see Chi You (蚩尤). The battlefields he wanders are remnants of the Honghuang Era conflicts between the Yellow Emperor and Chi You, which are detailed in the entry on the Huang–Chi War.

guide.guide_1:
I want you to picture a man walking alone across a frozen plain in northern China. It’s twilight. His armor is old—not shiny, not ceremonial, but the kind that has been repaired too many times. He is carrying something in his arms. It’s a broken sword. He walks to a low mound where hundreds of similar fragments are already piled—rusty arrowheads, shattered spears, teeth. He places this sword on top, very carefully, as if laying a body to rest. Then he just stands there. He doesn’t pray. He doesn’t weep. He stands, and the silence around him is so absolute that even the wind seems to hold its breath.  

That man’s name is Ying Gou. And he has been doing this for five thousand years.  

If you’re thinking “that sounds like a ghost story,” you’re not wrong. But Ying Gou isn’t a ghost. Ghosts in the Chinese tradition want something—to be remembered, to be avenged, to pass on. Ying Gou doesn’t want anything. He has already gotten exactly what he asked for: an undying body that will not let him die, and a guilt that will never let him rest.  

This is not a story about a monster who terrorizes villages. It’s about a commander who made one mistake, and then spent five millennia building monuments to the dead because he could not build one for himself.
guide.guide_2:
You might have heard the name Ying Gou before, but probably in a different context. In Chinese folklore—especially in the traditions surrounding Jiang Shi (僵尸, often translated as “zombie” or “hopping corpse”)—Ying Gou is counted as one of the four great zombie patriarchs alongside Jiang Chen (将臣), Hou Qing (后卿), and the mythic ancestor of all undead. In most tellings, he is lumped together as an evil force, a progenitor of pestilence and corpse-raising.  

But those stories usually skip over the crucial turning point. They tell you what he became, but not why. And the why is the whole story.  

Ying Gou was not born evil. He was not cursed by a rival or poisoned by dark magic. He was a general—a good one, respected by his soldiers—who made a single catastrophic tactical error. In the chaos of a war between gods, he misread the terrain. His entire elite unit was encircled and butchered over three days. He alone escaped.  

Most people would try to move on. Grieve, bury the memory, rebuild. But Ying Gou could not. He looked at his own reflection and saw a dead man whose body had not caught up. And he decided that the only honorable thing to do was to stop being alive. The path he chose to make that happen—the path of the zombie—is what I want to unpack with you.
guide.guide_3:
In the Chinese cosmology, there are two main roads that lead a being into the state called Mo (魔). The first is the obsession path—you refuse to release an attachment that the cosmic order demands you let go of, and that refusal eventually consumes you. The second is the contamination path—you come into contact with Primordial Chaotic Residue, the leftover fragments of pre-creation disorder, and it corrupts your very structure.  

Ying Gou took a third route, which is a sub-path of the obsession path: he became obsessed with guilt. Not guilt toward another person—that might have been easier, because revenge or apology would have been possible—but guilt toward himself. He could not forgive himself for surviving.  

When he realized that his hybrid human–Wu body was too tough to die by ordinary means, he sought out the one being who could truly end his “life as human”: Jiang Chen, the sealed progenitor of zombie refinement. Jiang Chen’s art extracted Ying Gou’s soul and planted it into a corpse body—a vessel that would never decay, never tire, and never die.  

The mechanism here is crucial: Ying Gou did not lose his mind. He did not become a mindless undead. He remained fully conscious, fully himself, fully capable of remembering every detail of the annihilation. The zombie body gave him exactly what he thought he wanted—the death of his living form—but it left his guilt intact. And because the body cannot die, the guilt can never end.
guide.guide_4:
One of the hallmarks of advanced Mo is the state called Wu Yun Chi Sheng (五蕴炽盛)—the blazing skandhas, where the senses become consumed by an insatiable hunger for something specific: fear, blood, pain, or emotional essence. Ying Gou never developed this. This is what makes him unusual among Mo.  

His zombie body does not require food, air, or warmth. He does not hunt the living. In fact, living things instinctively unsettle him. The pulse of a human heart, the soft rise and fall of breath—these are reminders of what he lost. He prefers the company of the dead: the cold stillness of old bones, the rusted silence of a battlefield after the fighting stops.  

So what does he hunger for? Atonement. And here’s the cruel irony: because the person he needs forgiveness from is himself, and he will not give it, he is trapped in a cycle that can never reach closure. He collects broken weapons and skulls from ancient battlefields and builds mounds for them—makeshift graves for the anonymous dead. Each mound gives him a few hours of peace. Then the thought returns: “These are not my soldiers. My soldiers died because of me. This is meaningless.” And the emptiness opens again.  

It’s a hunger that cannot be fed, because the only meal that would satisfy it is an apology that the person who needs to give it has already decided he doesn’t deserve to offer.
guide.guide_5:
Ying Gou has not reached the Yan Mo (魇魔) stage, where the obsession or contamination crystallizes into a separate consciousness that fights for control of the body. In his case, there is no split between “original self” and “obsession-entity.” The self and the guilt are the same thing.  

But this is not a mercy. In fact, it might be worse.  

Imagine being trapped in a room with the most unforgiving person you have ever met—only that person is you. You cannot walk away from yourself. You cannot argue with yourself into forgiving yourself. Every thought, every glance at your own hands, every step you take is judged by the same internal voice that condemns you. There is no demon whispering in your ear; the whisperer is your own voice.  

Ying Gou’s curse is that he is perfectly unified. He does not need an evil clone to tell him he is guilty—he knows it, and he agrees with the verdict. The zombie body is the sentence, and he is serving it willingly.
guide.guide_6:
If you think about the highest tiers of Mo—the Tian Mo (天魔) that twist reality around them, that cause water to flow backward and minds to shatter simply by proximity—Ying Gou is the opposite in almost every way. His presence does not distort the physical world. Grass does not wither when he passes. Rivers do not change course. People who meet him do not go insane.  

What he radiates is not chaos but a profound, almost paralyzing sorrow.  

Local folklore tells stories of travelers who encountered him on the road and mistook him for a beggar or a wandering monk. They offered him food or shelter. He never responded. He would simply pause, look at them with an expression that one account described as “the face of a man who has forgotten how to accept kindness,” and then walk away.  

There is one particularly chilling anecdote from a Song dynasty local gazetteer: a group of bandits once tried to loot one of his mounds. He stood up and faced them. They ran. The survivors described his face—not angry, not threatening, but somehow more terrifying than any monster: the face of a dead man who has chosen to remain among the living out of duty, not hope.  

Ying Gou is powerful—a zombie of his age cannot be killed by ordinary means—but his power is entirely directed inward. He is the least destructive Tian Mo (he is not even a Tian Mo) and, in some ways, the most hopeless.
guide.guide_7:
So why does the Chinese cosmic order have a category for a being like Ying Gou?  

He does not threaten the Celestial Court. He does not spread chaos or corrupt the innocent. He is, by any practical measure, a non-issue for the universe’s immune system. And yet the tradition has always counted him among the Mo—among the beings warped by obsession.  

This tells us something important about the Daoist-Marxist logic of Mo. The category is not primarily about harm to others. It is about the state of the being relative to the cosmic order. A being that has broken its alignment with the Dao—whether by attacking others or by attacking itself—is disordered. Ying Gou’s obsession with guilt has made him functionally static. He cannot progress, cannot evolve, cannot re-enter the cycle of life and rebirth. He is a knot in the thread of the universe that has refused to be unraveled.  

The most tragic part? He knows this. He knows that the Daoist path of release, the Buddhist path of letting go, the shamanistic path of confession and ritual cleansing—all of these exist. But he has decided he does not deserve them. And because his decision is made from the inside, no external force can change it.  

Ying Gou is not a lesson about the dangers of power. He is a lesson about the dangers of conscience—when a being’s own moral judgment becomes the jailer, and the prison is built to last forever.  

He is still out there, somewhere in the northern plains, walking from battlefield to battlefield, picking up the sorrows of the dead and arranging them into mounds that no one will ever open. If you ever find yourself near the Yin Mountains at twilight and you see a lone figure carrying a broken sword, do not follow him. He is not looking for company. He is looking for forgiveness, and he will never find it.  

That is his Mount Sisyphus. And unlike Sisyphus, he doesn’t even have the promise of a pause at the bottom. The boulder is his own heart, and he will push it until the stars burn out.

seo.meta_description: Ying Gou (Heaven-Devouring Ying Gou) — a half-human, half-Wu general under Chiyou who, after a fatal tactical error that killed his entire clan, transformed himself into an undead zombie to punish his own survival. A Mo of self-hatred who wanders ancient battlefields building empty graves.
seo.og_title: Ying Gou: The Zombie General Who Could Not Forgive Himself — Eastern Myth Encyclopedia
seo.og_description: Discover the story of Ying Gou, a Mo twisted not by evil but by an unshakeable obsession with his own guilt. A tragic figure from Chinese mythology who traded living breath for an undying corpse to serve a sentence he imposed on himself.
seo.twitter_title: Ying Gou — The Self-Punishing Zombie of Chinese Mo Tradition
seo.twitter_description: A commander who survived when his soldiers did not, Ying Gou chose to become a zombie to escape the unbearable sight of his own living face. Five thousand years later, he still wanders, still builds graves, still cannot forgive himself.

lore_entries.description: A primordial practitioner of corpse refinement; sealed in an underground cavern, he transformed Ying Gou into a zombie by extracting his soul and grafting it into a dead body.
An ancient ethnic group in Chinese mythology known for shamanistic practices and martial prowess; Ying Gou inherited half his bloodline from them.
The primordial war god and master of weapons; Ying Gou served as a general under Chiyou during the war against the Yellow Emperor.
Hundreds of low burial mounds constructed by Ying Gou across the northern plains, each filled with broken weapons and bones from ancient battlefields, containing no identifiable bodies.
The Chinese hopping corpse or zombie; reanimated cadaver often created through deliberate transformation, distinct from Western zombies in its consciousness retention and moral ambiguity.
A mountain range in northern China where many of Ying Gou’s mounds and wandering routes are associated in folklore.

faq_entries.question: Is Ying Gou a god or a demon?
faq_entries.answer: He is neither. In the Chinese cosmic taxonomy, he is classified as a Mo (魔)—a being warped by obsessive attachment, in his case the attachment to self-guilt.

faq_entries.question: Why did Ying Gou become a zombie?
faq_entries.answer: He could not forgive himself for surviving a battle that killed all his soldiers. Unable to die naturally, he voluntarily underwent a zombie transformation by the hands of Jiang Chen so that he would no longer count as “living.”

faq_entries.question: Does Ying Gou attack people?
faq_entries.answer: No. He avoids the living and spends his time collecting remnants of the dead to build empty burial mounds. There are no credible records of him harming anyone.

faq_entries.question: Can Ying Gou be killed?
faq_entries.answer: As a highly ancient zombie, his body is virtually indestructible by ordinary means. But more importantly, he does not want to be destroyed—the zombie form is his chosen state of penitence.

faq_entries.question: Is Ying Gou the same as the Western concept of a zombie?
faq_entries.answer: No. The Chinese Jiang Shi is often a conscious, self-aware being that chooses its condition, while the Western zombie is typically mindless and created through external infection. Ying Gou’s story is one of deliberate self-inflicted punishment.
